system_description.narrative_title: Fragmented Power: Tech Rivalry, Regional Wars and Macro Stress
system_description.narrative_summary: The global order is an open, tightly coupled system in flux where great‑power tech competition (especially US‑China over AI chips) intersects with regional security shocks (Iran, Russia‑Ukraine, Gaza) to drive commodity, supply‑chain and alliance shifts. Sticky inflation and hawkish central banks amplify financial volatility, while corporate governance and espionage episodes (notably in semiconductor firms) create political spillovers that reshape trade controls and diplomacy. Actors improvise through ad‑hoc diplomacy and market adjustments, producing fragile de‑escalations alongside persistent structural risk.
system_description.scope: Major-state interactions (US, China, Russia, EU, Iran, Gulf states, Israel, Ukraine), allied security arrangements (NATO, G7), global markets (energy, commodities, bonds, FX, equity), critical technology and supply chains (semiconductors, AI hardware, rare earths), transnational incidents (espionage, strikes, shipping attacks), and diplomatic/peace negotiation processes.
system_description.super_system: The planetary international political‑economic system: the integrated global order of interstate relations, transnational markets, technological infrastructures, and environmental‑security constraints.
adjacent_subsystems: Global Financial System (bond markets, FX, central bank policy and inflation dynamics)
Global Energy & Maritime Security System (oil, LNG, pipelines, shipping routes like Hormuz)
Global Technology & Supply‑Chain System (semiconductor production, AI deployment, rare earths, corporate governance)
Regional Security Complexes (Middle East, Eastern Europe, East Asia/Taiwan tensions)

variables.name: US–China technology and chip competition
variables.description: The United States, China and multinational tech firms are contesting dominance in semiconductors and AI, with export controls, corporate-security scandals and policy shifts driving partial decoupling of supply chains and market access rules.

variables.name: Russia–Ukraine war and negotiation dynamics
variables.description: Russia, Ukraine and their external backers are locked in an episodic high-intensity conflict even as intermittent diplomacy and prisoner swaps reshape bargaining positions and the prospects for a negotiated settlement.

variables.name: Iran–Gulf maritime and regional escalation
variables.description: Iran, Gulf states, the United States and regional proxies (including the Houthis) are engaged in strikes, island exchanges and base-level pressures that are increasing maritime security risks and episodic military escalation in the Gulf region.

variables.name: Global monetary tightening and bond-market stress
variables.description: Major central banks (led by the US Fed) and global investors are driving higher interest rates and volatile sovereign bond markets, shifting financial conditions, capital flows and macroeconomic policy trade-offs worldwide.

variables.name: European security realignment and architecture debates
variables.description: European governments, NATO and the United States are renegotiating defence postures, new security hubs and possible engagement with Russia, producing realignment pressures and intra‑Western debate over burden‑sharing and strategic frameworks.
